activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through an extra loop of tubing, making the air column longer and the note lower.
story:
Maelie had been in band for three weeks, and the trumpet still made no sense to her. Three valves. Seven fingerings she was supposed to know. But every time she played a C and then a D, something went wrong, and Mr. Mwangi would stop the whole group and ask her to check her fingering again.

After class she stayed behind while Issac packed his trombone and Giuseppe snapped his clarinet case shut. The old trumpet she was borrowing sat on the stand, dented and dull, the one Giuseppe called "the Emperor" because it had belonged to some player who never missed a note, according to legend anyway.

"How do three buttons make all those notes?" she asked.

Issac shrugged. "You just memorize them."

That answer annoyed her. She set the Emperor on her lap and pressed the second valve down, then the first, one at a time, blowing a soft note each time. The second valve made the note a little lower. The first valve made it lower still. She tried pressing the second valve and, right before she blew, pulled its little slide out a few centimetres, like a drawer opening. The note sank even further than before.

"Giuseppe, come listen." She played the note with the slide pushed in, then with it pulled out. "Does the second one sound lower?"

"Way lower," Giuseppe said.

"So pressing a valve isn't magic. The valve just shoves the air down an extra loop of tubing. Longer tube, lower note. And if I pull the slide out, the loop gets even longer." It was the most logical thing she had found all month. If a note was too high, she might be able to salvage it with her slide instead of lipping it down the way Mr. Mwangi kept telling her to.

She tried her C again. It had been sharp all week. She pulled the main tuning slide out a tiny bit, blew, listened, pulled it a little more. On the third try the needle on Issac's tuner app sat dead centre. Her C was finally in tune, and she hadn't changed her lips at all.

Then Issac leaned over and squinted into the bell. "Maelie. Somebody already cranked that slide way out before you. Like, way out. Whoever had the Emperor last was tuning it for a freezing cold room, or they had no idea what they were doing."

Maelie pulled the slide the rest of the way out, turned it over, and found a strip of masking tape with faded writing along the side: DO NOT TOUCH, E.M.

"Who's E.M.?" she asked.

Giuseppe went quiet for a second. "Mr. Mwangi's initials are Elliot Mwangi."

She looked at the tape, then at the door Mr. Mwangi had just walked out of. "Then he's the one who couldn't tune a trumpet."

Issac said, "Play the C again. Right now. Before he comes back."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah, or hanukkiah, has nine branches: eight for the eight nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others.
story:
Gabrielle stood on a chair in the community hall, draping a paper chain along the stage, when her little cousin marched up holding a menorah he had built out of clay and birthday candles.

"Count my candles," he demanded. "I made it perfect."

She counted. One, two, three, all the way to eight. "That's the eight nights," she said. Something tickled the back of her mind, though. Every menorah she had ever seen at their synagogue had one more candle than that, sitting higher or off to the side, like a supervisor. Why would her cousin's look different?

Before she could puzzle it out, the hall doors banged open and Samuelle came in with a foil pan of her mother's latkes. Samuelle had never been to a Hanukkah party before, and she wandered the room like it was a museum, squinting at the dreidels and the sufganiyot dusted with powdered sugar. Then she stopped in front of the big silver menorah on the long table.

"Wait," Samuelle said. "Hanukkah is eight nights, right? So why does that thing have nine candles?"

"That's the question of the evening," Gabrielle said. "My cousin built one with eight and now I'm suspicious of both of them." She lifted the silver menorah down and set it on the table between them. "There has to be a reason. Things in traditions usually have reasons, even weird ones."

She counted the branches out loud, tapping each one with a fingernail. Eight of them stood in a neat row, all the same height. The ninth sat apart, raised above the others like it had won a trophy. Gabrielle turned the menorah slowly, looking at it from every angle, wondering what that odd candle did all by itself. Then she noticed the wax drips. The eight lower cups were clean, barely used. The tall one was caked with old wax, burned down again and again.

"It lights the others," she said slowly. "It's the only one that gets used every single night, so it's the only one that's a mess. The other eight just hold the candles for each night."

Just then the rabbi's wife walked by, balancing a tray of candles, and Gabrielle caught her sleeve. "The tall one, the helper candle, is there a name for it?"

"The shamash," the woman said, and moved on toward the kitchen.

Samuelle tried it out. "Shamash." She grinned. "So the ninth candle is basically the employee of the month."

"The very obstinate employee," Gabrielle said. "It works every night and never gets a night off." She turned to her cousin, who was guarding his clay creation under the treat table like a dragon. "Your menorah needs a ninth branch," she told him. "For the shamash."

"No," he said, arms crossed. "Eight is perfect. Eight nights, eight candles. We made a treaty and I shook on it with myself."

Gabrielle devised a plan on the spot. She traded him a jelly donut for one birthday candle and a lump of his leftover clay, then stood back while he jammed a wobbly ninth candle onto the roof of his creation, higher than all the rest, exactly where a helper belonged.

"There," she said, and lit it first.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: In the beep test, or multistage fitness test, runners go back and forth between markers usually 20 meters apart, and the beeps come faster at each new level.
story:
Ella found out about the beep test on Monday, when Ms. Kaminski taped a sheet to the gym door listing what Thursday's tryouts would include. Kye read it over her shoulder and groaned. "Not the beep test," he said. "I failed that in thirty seconds last year."

That night Ella called Sloan, who had made the team the year before. Sloan had gone straight to the point. "You run back and forth between two markers, twenty meters apart," she said, "and the beeps come faster at each new level." Then she hung up because her mom was calling her to dinner. Ella sat on her bed turning it over in her head. Last year she had watched Kye sprint the first lengths like a rabbit and then die out by level four. Maybe the problem wasn't speed at all. Maybe it was the pacing. If the beeps sped up, then running flat out early would leave nothing for later, like blowing all your allowance on Monday.

So she devised a plan and wrote it on the back of a cereal box: do not get to the marker early. Get there just before the beep, turn, and go again. Tuesday after school she set out two buckets in the backyard, twenty meters apart, which took some measuring with a tape from the garage and a lot of walking back and forth. Her little brother watched from the porch and offered to honk a bike horn at random, which Ella declined. She used a timer app instead, set to beep at intervals she made shorter as she went. She kept her pace so even it almost felt slow. When the beeps got faster, she let herself speed up, little by little, saving something in her legs.

On Wednesday she did it again, and this time when the clock on the kitchen wall showed the minute hand had made nearly a whole revolution, she was still running. Her legs burned, but she noticed something else too: the intervals she had guessed for the later levels were close to the real ones, because she was still arriving just before each beep instead of long before or long after.

Thursday at tryouts, the gym smelled like floor wax. When the beeps started, Kye shot off the line like it was a sprint race, and by level three he was bent over with his hands on his knees. Ella held back, crossed each line a heartbeat ahead of the sound, turned, and went again. Level five. Level six. The beeps closed in like a tightening net, and she rose to meet them each time.

When she finally missed two in a row, Ms. Kaminski clicked her stopwatch and looked down at her clipboard, then back at Ella. "Level seven," she said. "Same as Sloan last year." Ella walked to the wall, slid down it, and grinned at Kye. "Next time," she panted, "run with me."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Article 1 of Germany's Basic Law, its constitution since 1949, begins with the words 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'
story:
The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Anthony's worksheet had one blank line left: Explain one right from Canada's Charter of Rights and Freedoms in your own words. He had written "freedom of expression" at the top, and then nothing, because every time he tried to put it in his own words the sentence fell apart like wet sand.

"You're staring at that line like it insulted you," Lya said, peering over his shoulder in the hallway outside courtroom four.

"It's the 'in your own words' part. Ms. Wong said we can't just copy the Charter. But the Charter already used up all the good words."

Lya sat down on the bench beside him. "My cousins live in Germany, and they showed me their constitution when I visited. It's called the Basic Law, and it's been their constitution since 1949. Guess what Article 1 says. 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.'"

Anthony looked up. "Inviolable?"

"Their whole constitution starts with dignity. Ours starts with rights and freedoms." She tapped his worksheet. "Different doors into the same house, maybe."

Ethan slumped onto the bench on Anthony's other side. "This assignment is impossible. There's no right answer, so there's no way to know if you're right." He said it like the day was already ruined, which was how he said most things.

Anthony didn't answer right away. He was thinking about the German line, how a whole country had decided the first thing worth writing down was that nobody could trample a person's dignity. Maybe the trick wasn't to find fancy words. Maybe it was to say what the right actually did. He tested it out, quietly, on the blank line: Expression means you can say what you think, and the government can't shut the valve on it just because it opposes you.

"That's it?" Ethan said, reading it upside down. "That's your answer? It's so... plain."

"That's the point, maybe."

Ms. Wong called them into the courtroom, where a lawyer was waiting to answer questions. When it was Anthony's turn, he read his sentence out loud, and the lawyer said, "That's as good a summary as I've heard. Plain is what the law is supposed to be."

Ethan pulled out his worksheet, crossed out nothing, but kept writing. Anthony watched him fill three lines, then four, then tug Lya's sleeve. "Hey, tell me the German one again. About dignity."

Lya leaned over and whispered it, word by word.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
story:
Sebastian stood at the gate of the nature reserve with his mandatory field trip form crushed in his fist, but he was not thinking about the form. He was thinking about the painting he had glimpsed through the window of the old museum barn, because the class was headed there next. In the painting, a dog covered in black spots sat beside a shining red fire engine, and Sebastian could not stop wondering why.

"How can there be a fire station thing out here?" Jamie asked as they walked the gravel path. "This is a nature reserve. There are herons."

"Maybe the barn is older than the reserve," Sebastian said. "Ms. Sok said the land used to belong to a village." That would make sense, he thought. Old places keep old things.

Inside the barn, the engine sat under a layer of dust, and beside it a wooden carriage with tall spoked wheels and long poles where two horses would have stood. Gael pointed at the painting. "Why would they hang a picture of a spotted dog next to an old fire engine? That's the anomaly here. Nothing else in this barn is about dogs."

"Firehouse dog," said the ranger quietly, already moving on toward the paddock. Sebastian did not get more than that, and it bugged him all through the nature walk. A firehouse dog. But why spots? Why a dog at all? He turned it over while the class counted frogs in the marsh, and one detail kept snagging on his mind: the carriage had no motor. The poles meant horses.

At the paddock, two heavy draft horses dozed in the sun. The ranger's own dog, an actual Dalmatian named Pongo, trotted over from the shed, and Sebastian watched closely. He expected the horses to shy, the way they sometimes did at the class's loud voices. Instead both horses lowered their heads toward Pongo, ears soft, and Pongo leaned against a gray shoulder like they were old friends.

That was his clue. "They get along," Sebastian said. "The dog and the horses. Ms. Sok, can I test something?" She nodded, so he asked the ranger if he could walk Pongo along the fence. The dog trotted ahead of him, and when Sebastian stopped, Pongo kept going, running up the path in front of him, turning to check that he followed, clearing the way the way a guide does. Behind him Sebastian heard the horses whinny and pace the fence, wanting to come along.

"So maybe that's it," Sebastian said, half to himself, half to Jamie and Gael, who had followed. "The engines didn't always have motors. Fire carriages were pulled by horses, and the dog got along well with horses and ran ahead, helping clear the way. That's why firehouses wanted spotted dogs." He said it out loud because saying it made the pieces fit, and the painting in the barn suddenly made sense too.

"Prove it," Gael said, grinning. So Sebastian retrieved Pongo's lead rope from the hook by the shed, clipped it on, and walked toward the old carriage barn with the dog trotting out in front of him, exactly like in the painting.

"Look," Sebastian said, pointing at the canvas. "The dog's out front, ahead of the horses. It was always out front."

Jamie leaned closer to the painted wheels and whispered, "I'm never calling a firehouse dog weird again."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
story:
Jace set the sheet music on the piano stand and read the note taped to the top of the page again. It was from his friend Mahdi, written in his terrible handwriting: "Mr. Whitehead says if we crash at the recital tomorrow because you play the middle part too fast, I will personally hide your sneakers in the gym ceiling. Practice slow. Andante exists for a reason."

The problem was that Jace did not know what andante meant. He knew largo and allegro too, the strange words printed above the staff like tiny road signs, but none of them came with translations. He had guessed before, in band class, that andante meant fast, because the word looked like "athletic." The middle section of the piece had collapsed into a pile of clashing notes, and Bodie, who played trumpet, had leaned over and whispered, "Bro, you just endangered the whole song." That was yesterday. The recital was tomorrow at four o'clock, which gave Jace one evening to figure it out.

He tried an experiment. He set his phone on the piano with a metronome app open and played the largo section first, as slowly as he could stand, letting the chords stretch out like taffy. Slow actually felt right for the opening, grand and heavy. Then he reached the word allegro and pushed the tempo up, quick and bouncy, and the melody came alive. He inhaled, held his breath, and started the andante section at the same fast speed. Within four measures his hands tangled and he lost his place entirely, exactly like in class.

So andante was not fast. That much was clear from the wreckage. He texted Mahdi, and the reply came fast: "my sister says largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively. she says you're welcome. she also says who is the protagonist of that piece, you or the metronome?" Jace laughed out loud in the empty living room. Walking pace. Not a stroll, not a sprint, just walking.

He tried it, tapping his foot like footsteps on a sidewalk, and the middle section finally made sense. The melody had room to breathe between the slow beginning and the flying end. He played the whole piece through three times, and on the third time he only stumbled once, at the page turn.

At nine o'clock he texted Mahdi a photo of the music with all three words circled. The answer came back in seconds: "good. your sneakers are safe for now. see you at four, walking pace."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Natural selection requires three things: individuals that vary, traits that are inherited, and some variations helping individuals survive and reproduce more than others.
story:
Landon spread his notebook across the kitchen table and drew a fat parrot beak, a thin warbler beak and a crushing ground finch beak, one above the other. His little sister pulled her chair up beside him because whenever Landon drew anything, she wanted to see it.

"These are finches," he said. "Same birds, different islands. Some islands have big hard seeds, and the birds there have thick strong beaks. On islands with small soft insects, the beaks are thin." He tapped his pencil on the page. "Look how each beak shape corresponds to the food on its island. Like a key matching its lock."

"Why don't the thin-beak birds just move?" she asked.

That was actually a good question, and Landon had to think about it. Ms. Bianchi had made the class memorize three things that all had to be true before you could call something natural selection, and tomorrow there was a quiz. "They don't exactly choose," he said slowly. "Here, help me check." He wrote three boxes. "First, do the birds vary? Do some have thicker beaks than others, even on the same island?"

"Like I'm taller than my friend even though we're the same age," his sister said.

"Right, exactly." He checked the first box. "Second, are beak shapes inherited? Do thick-beaked parents have thick-beaked chicks?"

"The baby birds look like their parents. I've seen that."

He checked the second box and hesitated on the third. He almost wrote it down, then stopped. Maybe he should test it instead of just saying it. He grabbed a handful of dried beans and a handful of rice from the cupboard and put them in two bowls. "Use only these tweezers and pick up beans for thirty seconds. Then use the spoon." His sister clicked the tweezers and got three beans; with the spoon she scooped nineteen. "So on a bean island," Landon said, "the spoon birds survive better and have more chicks. On a rice island, the tweezers win."

"That's the third thing," his sister said. "Some beaks help them survive and have more babies than others."

Landon checked the last box and sat back. All three. Only when all three were true did it count as natural selection, and now he could see why, because if the beaks weren't inherited, or if nothing survived better, nothing would change over time. He copied his three boxes onto a clean page so he could redraw them from memory later.

Their father came through the kitchen, looked at the beans and rice scattered across the table, and raised one eyebrow. "You two are negotiating a peace treaty with the pantry?"

"No," Landon said, grinning. "We're being diplomats between a bean island and a rice island." His sister laughed so hard she knocked over the bean bowl, and the beans rolled everywhere, dormant little seeds waiting for an island that would never come. Landon chased the last one under the toaster and added one more drawing to his page: a spoon-shaped beak.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: German has one word, "Geschwister," for brothers and sisters together, the way English uses "siblings."
story:
On Thursday, German class got a new assignment, and Nora copied it into her notebook with a sinking feeling: describe your family and pets in five full sentences, due Monday. She could handle "Ich habe einen Hund" and "Meine Mutter ist freundlich," but five whole sentences felt like a mountain. Mr. Henry had said the trick was not translating English word by word, and Nora wondered what that meant. German had to have its own shortcuts, didn't it? She wanted to find one.

She cornered Mathias at lunch, because Mathias had three brothers and a sister and had been complaining about the same assignment all morning. "I'm going to be writing forever," he groaned, stabbing his fork into his pasta. "Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe eine Schwester. My hand is going to fall off." Nora slid her notebook across the table. What if the language had a shorter path, some formula like the ones in math, where a big thing collapses into one tidy expression? She underlined his four sentences and stared at them, tapping her pencil. Four sentences about siblings. There had to be a way to say it once.

After school they found Mr. Henry loading boxes into his car, and Nora asked him straight out. "Is there one word for brothers and sisters together? Like, all of them at once?" He smiled and shut the trunk. "Geschwister," he said, and spelled it for them. Then he drove off, leaving them standing in the parking lot with the word hanging in the air. Nora wrote it down three times so she wouldn't lose it. So German used Geschwister the way English used siblings, one word covering everyone, and that fact changed the whole shape of her homework. She could describe the relationships in a single stroke and spend her energy on the rest.

The catch was the grammar. Geschwister looked plural to Nora, so she tried "Ich habe vier Geschwister" and then hesitated, because what if the verb changed, or what if it needed different articles than she expected? Getting it wrong in front of the class on Monday would make her feel exposed, vulnerable in a way that answering a math problem wrong never did. She decided to test it. She wrote her sentence, then flipped it around into a question, "Hast du Geschwister?", and practiced it on Elyse outside the library, pretending they were two strangers meeting in Berlin.

Monday arrived. Mathias went first, and Nora held her breath as he said, "Ich habe vier Geschwister," instead of four separate sentences. Mr. Henry nodded and marked something in his book, and Nora let out her breath. When her turn came, she stood up, articulated her five sentences slowly and carefully, and finished with "Ich habe zwei Geschwister und einen Hund." Mr. Henry wrote a check mark beside her name. Walking back to her seat, she caught Mathias's eye and mouthed the new word. "Geschwister," he whispered back.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
story:
Saturday morning, Liam stood in his kitchen with his boots still wet from the precipitation that had been falling since dawn, staring at the flyer on the fridge. Volunteer day, the food bank on Miller Street, ten o'clock. He had promised his mom he would try it once, and now that the moment had arrived, he kind of wished the rain had turned into a full snowstorm so staying home would seem reasonable.

The food bank turned out to be a bright room in the basement of a church, with long metal shelves and a smell of cardboard and apples. Ms. Pelletier handed him a clipboard and a pair of reading glasses on a cord. "The dates on the cans are tiny," she said. "Wear these. They magnify the print so you can check nothing has expired." Liam put them on, and the little stamped numbers jumped out at him, sharp and sudden, like the world had leaned in closer. Chase was already at the next shelf, racing through soup cans and calling out dates like a game show host.

Halfway through the morning, Alanna looked up from her box of pasta. "Does anyone know how long food banks have even existed in Canada?" she asked. "Like, are they super old, or new?"

Liam thought about it. The room was in an old church, but the shelves looked new, and the fridge had a shiny sticker from a grocery store fundraiser. "Probably new," he said. "Maybe twenty years? People only started needing them recently, right?"

Chase shook his head slowly. "My grandma talks about them from way back."

Liam decided to test his idea the way he tested anything: find the evidence. Near the door hung a bulletin board thick with old photos, so he went over and worked through them, oldest at the bottom. There were pictures of volunteers in clothes from decades ago, and then, right at the bottom corner, a yellowed newspaper clipping with a headline he read twice. Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta. Beneath it, someone had written in faded marker: It started here later than that, but not much.

"Alanna!" he called across the room. "Come see. Nineteen eighty-one. Edmonton, Alberta. That's the first one." Alanna came over, and Chase too, and the three of them crouched by the board while Liam read the clipping aloud one more time, just to be sure he had it right.

Near closing time, a man with a walker came in and took only a small bag, though Ms. Pelletier had offered him a full box. Liam watched him pause at the door, adjusting his grip, and noticed the handle of a second, empty tote bag folded over his arm. "Would a lighter second bag help?" Liam asked, and fetched one, packing it with the easy-to-carry things, juice boxes and crackers. The man smiled and said, "That's for my neighbour. She can't get down the stairs on Saturdays."

Liam carried the bag out to the bus stop for him, rain spitting lightly, his own hands empty and warm. "Same time next week?" Alanna called from the door, and Liam waved back and said, "Next week."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
story:
Riley stood on second base long after the last out, dragging his cleats through the dirt while the parents folded chairs along the foul line. The end-of-season party was supposed to start in twenty minutes, on folding tables behind the backstop, but nobody had moved yet. Koen sat on the pitcher's mound pulling up little tufts of grass, and Ajay was spinning a ball in his glove even though the game was over. Riley had thought everyone would be loud and happy. Instead the team drifted around the diamond like the whole season had left something unfinished.

He walked over and dropped onto the grass beside Koen. "Why does everyone look like we lost? We won." Koen shrugged. Ajay rolled the ball toward them. "It's not the game. Next year there's tryouts again, and half of us won't make the same team. Some kids are moving schools. It won't be this team anymore." Riley frowned. He had felt it too, that heavy quiet, and he had blamed the wind, which came across the brown outfield like cold air off a tundra, flattening everything it touched.

That night he looked it up, because the feeling had a shape to it and shapes had names. His older sister's group-work textbook was still on the shelf, and there it was: a psychologist named Tuckman had stages for how groups form, storm, and settle. Then, in 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, called adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. Riley read it twice. He had assumed something was wrong with them, that winning should feel clean and bright. It was a stage. Teams ended, and feeling strange about it was part of the ending, not a fault in the day.

At the party the next afternoon, behind the backstop, the same quiet hung over the pizza boxes. Riley set his cup down. "Adjourning," he said. Ajay blinked. "That's what it's called. In 1977 these two people, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen, added a fifth stage for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. It's a real thing. It's not just us being weird." Koen laughed, short and relieved. "So we're not sad, we're in stage five." "Basically," Riley said.

Ms. Suryanto, their neighbor who had volunteered as scorekeeper all season, raised her paper cup of lemonade from across the table. "To stage five, then," she said. The team clinked cups, paper against paper, and the quiet loosened. Ajay started retelling the double play from the fourth inning, waving his arms, and Koen argued the ball had bounced. Someone's little brother knocked over the cooler, and everyone rushed to save the ice. Riley bit into his slice, warm and folded, and listened to the voices pile up under the lights, which had not yet been switched off.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: The Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a state of purification after death before entering heaven, but most Protestant churches reject the idea.
story:
Jayden crouched beside the grave marker with a scrub brush in one hand and his notebook in the other. Mr. Morin had asked him to clean the lichen off his wife's headstone before the service at three, and it was already half past two. Shyanne and Payton had come along to help, mostly because Jayden had promised them the leftover donuts from his mom's box.

"I can do the left side," Shyanne said, kneeling and dipping her brush in the bucket. The water had gone gray, and a beetle crawled out from under the stone's base and headed for the grass.

Payton read the dates on the marker out loud. "Fifty-one years. That's a long marriage." He scrubbed at a patch of green with the edge of his sleeve.

A week ago, none of them would have been here. Jayden thought back to Sunday, when he'd sat in the back of Shyanne's church taking notes for his world religions project. He was supposed to compare how two faiths explained what happened after death, and he'd chosen Christianity and Buddhism because they seemed the most different. Then Payton had glanced at his notebook and frowned at the word Jayden had written down.

"What's purgatory?" Payton had asked.

Shyanne had blinked at him. "You don't know purgatory? You go to church every week."

"I've never heard the word in my life," Payton said. "It sounds like a counterfeit word, like somebody made it up to scare people."

That had been the start of the whole argument, and it was still going. The Catholic Church taught purgatory, a state of purification after death before entering heaven. Most Protestant churches, Payton's included, rejected the idea entirely. Jayden had written all this down, but Payton had insisted Shyanne's church must be wrong somewhere, and Shyanne had insisted he ask his own pastor, and somehow the argument had ended with all three of them agreeing to test it.

The test had been Jayden's idea, and it was simple: ask a second source. That was the rule for his project, the same rule that said you couldn't build a whole essay on one protagonist's point of view. So Payton had called his grandfather, who read the Bible every morning, and read him the question straight off Jayden's notebook. His grandfather had paused for a long time and then said, "Some churches teach that, we don't," which settled nothing and somehow settled everything. Two people, same book, different answers. Jayden had underlined that line twice.

Now the cemetery bell rang a quarter chime, and Mr. Morin's car turned in at the gate. The headstone was clean except for one gray patch near the bottom, and Shyanne dumped the rest of the bucket over it, letting the water submerge the stone's base and run off through the grass.

"They can both be right," Payton said suddenly, wringing out his rag. "About the big part, I mean. Heaven."

"Maybe," Shyanne said. "The purgatory part's the part we fight about."

"Write it both ways," Jayden said, snapping his notebook shut as the first mourners walked up the hill. "Two answers, one question."

Mr. Morin stopped beside the marker, put his hand flat on the clean granite, and said, "She'd have liked that you three worked on it together."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
story:
At dinner on Tuesday, Lucas pushed his noodles around the plate while his dad talked about the new bridge downtown, how its bones were steel alloyed with other metals to make it stronger than any single metal alone. Lucas wasn't really listening. He was thinking about the group chat, and about Aron.

It had started as a joke, Lucas supposed. Someone posted a picture of Aron's volcano project with a caption about how it looked like a pile of mud, and then everyone piled on, laughing emojis stacking up like a wall. Aron left the chat by fourth period. Lucas had wanted to say something, but every time he typed a message, he imagined the replies turning on him next, so he deleted his words and said nothing. When he finally decided to show the coach, the messages were already gone. Whoever sent them had deleted them, one by one, until the chat looked almost innocent.

"Something on your mind?" his mom asked. "You've stabbed those noodles about forty times."

Lucas set down his fork. "If someone says mean stuff in a chat and then deletes it, is it like it never happened?"

His dad tilted his head. "Depends. Anybody take a picture of it?"

The words landed, and a slow, bright idea opened in Lucas's mind. A screenshot. A screenshot froze the words before anyone could conceal them by deleting them. Messages could vanish, but a picture stayed. That was the pattern he'd been missing: the mean comments kept disappearing before an adult could see them, so no adult ever saw them. It wasn't that nobody cared. It was that nobody had a record.

He texted Adelaide under the table, pretending to check the time. Did you see what they posted about Aron before it got deleted? She wrote back within a minute: saw it, tried to show my sister, it was already gone. Lucas's thumb hovered. Then he typed: If it happens again, don't wait. Screenshot it. Even if it gets deleted, we'll still have proof to show Mr. Pérez. Then we tell him together, so it's not just one person against everyone.

Adelaide sent back a single thumbs-up, and then, after a pause, a longer message: Aron eats lunch in the library now. Somebody should sit with him.

Lucas looked up from his phone. His mom and dad were watching him with the particular patience of parents who know something is going on. "Can I be excused?" he asked. "I want to go online for a few minutes."

"As long as your homework's done," his dad said.

Lucas carried his plate to the sink, then walked back to the table and set his phone down where they could see the screen. "There's a kid in my class getting teased in a group chat," he said. It wasn't an eloquent speech, and his voice cracked in the middle, but he kept going anyway. "Tomorrow I'm going to sit with him at lunch, and if it starts again, I'll be ready."

His mom reached over and squeezed his hand. "Sounds like a plan," she said.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome, a ticking device that sets a steady tempo, in 1815.
story:
Sarah's band had a chronic problem, and nobody could say what it was. Every time they played "Moonrise March" in Joelle's garage, the song started fine and then fell apart somewhere in the middle, like a cake collapsing in the oven. Maddison blamed the drums. Joelle blamed Maddison. Sarah, who played the old upright piano against the back wall, said nothing, because she had a private suspicion that made her stomach drop: it was her.

She tested the idea at home, playing the march alone and recording it. When she listened back, the opening was steady, but by the second theme the notes were galloping, and by the big dynamic change, where the music was supposed to get quiet and mysterious, she was practically sprinting. So her rushing had to be the hidden cause. The others probably sped up to keep up with her, and the whole thing snowballed. But knowing that didn't fix it. She couldn't hear herself rushing while it happened, which felt like trying to watch her own back.

The next afternoon, Mr. Nkosi from next door was dragging lawn chairs into his truck when Sarah carried the trash out. He heard her humming the march and asked about it, and when she told him the problem, he disappeared into his house and came back with a small wooden box. Inside sat a brass pendulum that clicked when he wound it. "Metronome," he said. "Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815." He set the weight, and the ticking filled the air like a patient, mechanical heartbeat.

Sarah took it to the garage that evening, and the band gathered around it like it was a dragon egg. "What is that thing?" Maddison asked, poking the pendulum and nearly stopping it. Joelle wanted to know if it could do anything cooler than click. "It's from 1815," Maddison said, "so no." Sarah set it ticking at the march's tempo and they started over.

The first run-through was a disaster. Everyone watched the pendulum instead of playing, and Joelle hit a cymbal a full beat late, which sounded like a trash can falling downstairs. Sarah laughed so hard she had to stop. The second time, they ignored the ticking entirely, and the song collapsed at the same exact spot as always. Sarah noticed something then. The collapse always came right after the quiet section, the part where the dynamics dropped way down. When the music got soft, she leaned in, and leaning in made her hands rush, as if quiet meant fast instead of soft.

On the third try she made herself play the quiet section slowly on purpose, letting the click hold her back while the notes shrank to a whisper. It felt wrong, like walking through deep water, but the band stayed with her, and when the march swelled back to loud, they were still together, all four of them, right on the beat.

"Okay," Joelle said, wiping her forehead. "We keep the clicky box. It's in the band now. It can be our dynasty." Maddison reached over and slid the weight down the pendulum, and the ticking slowed, ominously, like time itself taking a nap. "Play it again," Sarah said, and cracked her knuckles.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Card stacking is showing only the facts that support one side while leaving out the facts against it, so the message seems stronger than it is.
story:
Ms. Gagnon had taped a tablet advertisement to the whiteboard, and Avery leaned forward in her seat because she wanted that exact tablet for her birthday, which was three weeks away. The ad listed five features in bold letters: a brilliant screen, a fast processor, a slim design, a free stylus, and a huge app store. "Who wants one of these?" Ms. Gagnon asked, and half the class raised their hands, including Zane and Audrey. "Notice how many hands went up," Ms. Gagnon said. "Advertisers notice too."

That was the bandwagon appeal, and Avery wrote it down. Then Ms. Gagnon played an old radio clip where a famous actor praised a brand of soup, calling it the finest cuisine in America, and Avery recognized a celebrity testimonial. Next came a wartime poster with loaded words like "coward" and "hero" splashed across terrified faces. The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the lemon floor cleaner the janitor used, and Avery's pencil was flying across her notebook.

After class, Audrey hurried after her into the hallway, where lockers slammed like thunder. "Did you raise your hand too?" Audrey asked. "For the tablet? Everyone's getting one." Avery hesitated. She had raised her hand, and now she felt an itch at the back of her mind, the same feeling she got when a math answer looked right but something underneath was off. At home that night, she found the tablet's official webpage and read every line. Screen, processor, design, stylus, apps. Five features, same five, over and over. What wasn't there?

She searched the model number plus the word battery, and the results filled the screen. Owners complained the battery barely lasted four hours on a charge, and one review called the screen beautiful but the battery life "a dealbreaker." The ad never mentioned it once. Avery sat back, the desk lamp warm on her hands, and understood what she was looking at: the ad showed only the facts that supported it and left out the facts against it, so it seemed stronger than it was. Zane had called it something in class while she was writing. She texted him: what's the word for when an ad only lists the good stuff?

"Card stacking," he typed back.

The next morning she showed her mom the ad, then the reviews. "It's not lying exactly," Avery said. "It's just showing one side." Her mom read both, tapping the counter, and said they'd look at other tablets together on Saturday, comparing everything, good and bad. When Avery told Audrey at lunch, Audrey stared at her tray. "I already told my parents that exact ad," she said, and her voice went small. "They ordered it last night." Avery put a hand on her shoulder to console her. "It's not too late," she said. "Cancel it, then show them what I found." Audrey picked up her phone.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The U.S. Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13, which is why many sites require users to be 13.
story:
The app was called Sparrow, and everyone in Mr. Hall's fifth period was on it except Nicholas. Beatrix had shown him her feed at lunch, a swirl of drawings and dodgeball videos, and now all he wanted was an account of his own. That evening he typed his real birthday, March 14, and the screen went red. "You must be 13 or older to use Sparrow," it said, in that flat way screens have of not arguing back.

He tried again the next morning in the school library, in case he had mistyped something. Same red message. He leaned over to Meliane, who was two seats away with her tablet. "It keeps asking for my birthday. Why does it even care?"

Meliane shrugged. "My cousin said something about a law. She said websites have to get your parents' permission before they can take your information if you're under 13. That's why most of them just say no one under 13 can join. Easier for them." She went back to her project on hummingbirds, which was due Friday and already six slides long. Nicholas sat with that. A law. From when, though, and who made it? He devised a plan on the back of his math worksheet: he would find the rule in writing, not just in a cousin's retelling.

He typed "why do apps ask if you are 13" into the library search. The answer came up fast, on a page about kids and the internet: the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, a United States law that requires parental consent before websites collect personal information from children under 13. He read the sentence twice. So that was the hidden rule under the red message. Sparrow wasn't being mean. It was dodging paperwork. He copied the name of the law into his notebook, letter by letter, because it seemed like the kind of thing a person should know exactly.

At lunch he found Beatrix by the window, defending her hummingbird slide notes from a drippy juice box. "The reason is a law from 1998," he said. "It says websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under 13. So they just make the age limit 13." Beatrix looked at him over her sandwich. "So if you put a different birthday..." "Then they'd be collecting my information without my parents knowing," Nicholas said. "That's the part that feels weird. It's not a lock, it's a rule."

Ms. Adeyemi, on lunch duty, had drifted close enough to hear the last part. She didn't lecture. She just said, "There's a permission form in the office for exactly this. Students use it all the time." Nicholas felt his grin go contagious; Beatrix caught it and grinned back, and even Meliane looked up from her hummingbirds, where a slide about nectar was waiting.

He got the form after last period, folded it into his backpack, and carried it home like something warm. "Mom," he called from the front door, waving the paper, "I need you to sign this."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: When David Rudisha set the men's 800-metre world record at the 2012 London Olympics, his first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second.
story:
Beatrice had lost her last three eight-hundred-metre races in the same strange way, and nobody could tell her why. She would lead after one lap, feeling wonderful, and then her legs would turn to something like wet sand and three people would pass her before the finish. Her coach only said, "Save something," which was the kind of advice that sounded like advice and worked like nothing at all.

Since the track was still locked for the season, she trained at the rink, running laps on the rubber walkway that circled the ice, where the cold air kept her from feeling like a boiled potato. Angelique stood by the boards with a stopwatch, shouting her splits, while Tayla sat on a cooler doing what Tayla did best, which was looking things up. "I found something," Tayla said one evening, holding out her phone. "David Rudisha's world record race. The 2012 Olympics. You can watch the whole thing."

They watched it right there, three heads bent over one small screen, while the Zamboni growled past behind them and the smell of cold rubber saturated everything. Rudisha ran from the front the entire way and won in a time so fast it looked like a typo. "Okay, so he never fades," Beatrice said. Tayla shook her head and tapped the lap times. "No. Look. His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second." Beatrice stared at the numbers. The world record holder, the best eight-hundred-metre runner who had ever lived, had also slowed down. Her dying second lap wasn't some freak phenomenon unique to her. It happened to everybody. The question was how much.

She tested it the next evening. Instead of attacking the first lap like a burglar who had forgotten something inside, she ran it deliberately, almost frugally, keeping something back the way her grandmother kept back the good chocolates. Angelique called out the split and Beatrice thought, that's slower than usual, this is a disaster. Then, on the second lap, her legs did not turn to wet sand. They stayed legs. She finished her final lap two seconds faster than she ever had before, and Angelique's shriek echoed off the ice hard enough that Mr. Friedman looked up from the skate rental counter and cupped a hand to his ear.

"You want to know the strangest part?" Beatrice said, hands on her knees, breath fogging in the rink air. "It felt easier and my time was better. That's basically cheating."

"Take it up with Rudisha," said Tayla.

Beatrice straightened up and pointed at the stopwatch. "Again. Right now. Angelique, count me down."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
The basketball court behind the school had painted lines all over it, and Raphael had figured out that one full loop around the outside fence was almost exactly four hundred metres, because he had counted his steps and done the math twice. Cindy sat on the bleachers with a stopwatch and a bag of pretzels, and Jasmin stood at the far corner holding a paper cone she had made to shout through.

"Three minutes!" Jasmin bellowed through the cone, which mostly made her sound like a duck. "You have to run eight hundred metres in three minutes by Friday, or Mr. Andersen says you can't be in the meet."

Raphael had been sprinting the first part of every practice run and then dying at the end, wobbling like a shopping cart with a bad wheel. The problem was that he could not see the thing that was beating him. It felt like his legs just quit on the second lap, but that made no sense, because his legs were the same legs he had started with. Something invisible had to be the cause, and he meant to hunt it down.

He devised a plan on the back of his race number, which he had pinned to his shirt inside out so the blank side showed. Three minutes for eight hundred metres on a four-hundred-metre track meant two laps, so he divided and got ninety seconds for the first lap. "Ninety seconds," he said, tapping the number with his pen. "If I do the first lap in ninety, I get the second lap in ninety too, and that's three minutes exactly."

"It feels slow," Cindy warned, when he jogged the first lap instead of charging off like a startled horse. "Like, birthday-parade slow."

"That's the illusion," Raphael puffed as he went by. "It feels easy now because I'm not burning everything up." He rounded the fence by the sagging net, waved at Jasmin, who honked her cone at him, and came through the first lap at ninety-one seconds. Then, instead of turning into a wobbly shopping cart, he stayed buoyant, almost light, and pushed the second lap hard enough to pass a very confused pigeon. He crossed the line, and Cindy pressed the stopwatch and yelled the time.

"Two minutes fifty-eight!" she shouted. "You did it! You did the thing!"

Jasmin ran over, still holding the cone, which now had a bite mark on it for reasons nobody asked about. "So the trick is going slow first?"

"Not slow," Raphael said, holding up the race number with the number ninety written on it, sweaty but readable. "Even. Ninety and ninety. I just have to do it again on Friday, only with seven other kids sprinting ahead of me like maniacs."

"Maniacs who will be walking by the end," Cindy said, and tossed him a pretzel, which he caught in his mouth.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: In summer, land heats up faster than the ocean, so warm air rises over the land and moist air from the ocean flows in to replace it.
story:
David carried the folded letter in his jacket pocket all the way up the trail, because it was the reason he had dragged Izaiah and Aikam out here on a Saturday at all. The letter was from his cousin in India, who had asked a question David could not stop thinking about: why does the rain arrive right when the heat is worst? He had to explain it in class on Monday, and so far all he had was a page of notes that said "monsoon" about nine times without saying anything else.

"Here," David said, stopping where the trail bent around a wide gray rock. He put his palm flat on the stone, then held it out toward the small stream below. "Rock feels hot. Water feels cold. Same sun all morning." He crouched and touched the stream. "The land heats up faster than the ocean. Like the rock and the water."

Aikam looked from the rock to the stream and back. "So?"

"So imagine the whole country is the rock." David pulled a notebook from his backpack and drew a lumpy shape for land and a wavy line for sea. "In summer, the land gets hot. Hot air rises, like over a campfire. When it rises over the land, air from the ocean flows in to take its place. And ocean air is wet air. That wet air comes in, and that's the rain." He tapped the drawing. "That's why the worst heat and the first rain show up together. The heat itself is pulling the rain in."

Izaiah frowned at the drawing. "You can't see air rising, though. How do you know you're not just making it up?"

David had been waiting for that. He tore off two strips of paper, wet one in the stream, and taped them to sticks a few steps apart, one over the hot rock and one over the shaded ground near the water. "Watch." The paper over the rock fluttered upward within a minute, curling and lifting on the rising heat, while the other strip hung still. "Temporary, it's only a demonstration," David admitted. "But it illustrates the idea. Mr. Farah says you can't see wind either, you see what it pushes."

Then came the twist. Aikam, who had been quiet, pulled out his phone. "My uncle farms rice near Dhaka. I texted him your rock thing last night." He held up the screen. "He says in the wet season the fields need that rain, and in the dry season they need the sun to dry the grain. Both. If the rain failed one year, the rice fails."

David stared at the message. He had been thinking of the monsoon as an answer to memorize, a line for the protagonist of his presentation to say, and here it was deciding whether his friend's family ate. He thought about how easily he could have copied a definition instead of climbing a hill to test it, and he still wasn't sure which choice had been the smarter one, only which one he would remember.

"Monday," he said, folding the notebook away, "I'm opening with the rock."

"You're opening with my uncle," Aikam said, holding the phone higher. "Read it out loud."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days.
story:
The bus groaned into the gravel lot of Willow Creek Pioneer Village just after ten in the morning, and Ms. Sokolov held up a clipboard before anyone could bolt for the gate. "Photo scavenger hunt," she said. "Teams of three, sheet due at the gatehouse at one fifteen, because the bus leaves at one thirty. Not one minute later." Jaxson grabbed Millie and Safa, his usual alliance, and they studied the sheet: a spinning wheel, a hand-forged nail, a working water pump, and one blank line marked "something the villagers did to survive summer."

They found the nail first, then the pump, where Safa took a turn cranking until cold water gushed over her sneakers and she shrieked with delight. Jaxson was already scanning the list again when he noticed the pigs. Behind a split-rail fence, three Berkshire pigs lay stretched in a black mud hole, and a fourth stood pressed against the far rails, trembling, its sides heaving fast. "That one looks sick," Millie said quietly. "It's shaking." The morning had been cool, but by noon the sun had turned the village into an oven, and the gravel crunched like burnt toast under their shoes.

Jaxson couldn't stop thinking about it while they photographed the spinning wheel. At ten, the pigs had all been rooting in the grass, ordinary and busy. At noon, three were buried in mud and one looked miserable. If the pig were sick, it would have acted strange all morning. But it had only gone wrong when the heat did. He compressed his empty water bottle into his pocket, refilled it at the pump, and led the others back to the fence. "Watch," he said, and poured a thin stream of water into a dusty hollow near the rails. The trembling pig heaved itself over, flopped into the wet spot, and rolled until its pink skin was brown.

"Okay, that was the opposite of sick," Safa said. A docent in a straw hat passed with a wheelbarrow and paused at the fence. "Smart pig," she said. "They've got very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days." She walked on, and Jaxson grinned so wide his face hurt. Millie checked her phone and gasped. "Twelve fifty. The gatehouse, now!"

They ran past the print shop, ducked under the low beam of the schoolhouse door, and skidded up to Ms. Sokolov just as the bus driver was starting the engine. Overhead, a wedge of migratory geese honked south across a hard blue sky, and Safa snapped one last picture while Jaxson scribbled on the blank line: "villagers' pigs kept cool in mud." Ms. Sokolov read it, then looked at the mud streaks on Jaxson's shoes and raised an eyebrow. "The pig did that," he said, breathless. "It was practically a science experiment." Millie held up the phone with the rolling pig mid-flop, and the bus doors hissed open behind them.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
story:
Victoria raised her hand before Ms. Campbell even finished explaining the game. "So we act out a scene, but nobody gets to plan it first?" Ms. Campbell nodded and said they would each draw a partner's name from the box. Victoria unfolded her slip of paper and read it twice: Samuel. He was the quietest kid in the class, the one who once went a whole week answering only in single words.

They started on the pretend beach, a couple of towels on the stage floor. "I found a message in a bottle," Victoria announced, holding up an invisible bottle. Samuel looked at his shoes. "Okay," he said. Nothing else came. Victoria speculated that maybe he hadn't heard her, so she repeated it louder. "Okay," Samuel said again, and the scene sat there like a car with the engine off. Across the stage, Mason and his partner were already arguing about whether an invisible shark could smell peanut butter, and the whole class was laughing.

Victoria tried three more offers. A seagull attack. A treasure map. A crab that could talk. Each time, Samuel agreed. "Sure." "Yeah." "Okay." The scene stalled every single time, and Victoria started to wonder if saying yes was actually the problem. It didn't make sense, because agreeing was supposed to be polite. But when she listened to Mason's scene, she noticed something. He never just agreed. When his partner said the shark was hungry, Mason said yes, and it was allergic to peanut butter, which is why it kept sneezing. Their scene grew like a snowball rolling downhill, while hers stayed a flat lump of sand.

"That's it," she whispered. Mason caught her eye during the break and grinned. "Yes, and," he said, wiggling his fingers like it was a magic spell. "You take what your partner gives, then you add something." Victoria turned back to Samuel, and instead of feeling annoyed, she noticed his hands were shaking a little, and his eyes kept darting toward the exit. He wasn't refusing her offers. He just didn't know how to build on them, and he was probably terrified of looking foolish in front of everyone.

She sat down beside him on the beach towel. "New plan," she said quietly. "I'll give you something so easy a robot could add to it. Watch." She stood, picked up the invisible bottle again, and held it out. "This message says our class is being attacked by a giant octopus. You're the one with the robust net, the strongest kid on the beach." Samuel blinked, then straightened up like someone had handed him a real job. "And the octopus," he said slowly, "is afraid of jellyfish." Victoria grabbed it instantly. "Yes, and look, a whole jar of jellyfish in my lunchbox!"

The class roared as the two of them chased the octopus around the towels, Samuel declaring himself the antagonist's worst nightmare, waving a net made of nothing at all. When Ms. Campbell called time, Samuel was out of breath and grinning, and Victoria realized the twist: the partner everyone thought would sink the scene had turned out to be the funniest one on the stage. "Same teams tomorrow?" Samuel asked. "Yes, and bring the jellyfish," Victoria said, tossing him the invisible jar.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A break statement stops a loop immediately, so a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor.
story:
Madison had forty minutes left before the coding showcase at Camp Birchwood, and her program was broken. She stared at the laptop screen in the craft cabin, where fifteen campers were typing in a hurry, fans humming in the window to push out the heat.

"Mine keeps saying 'not prime' a bunch of times," she said, tilting her screen toward Romane, who sat cross-legged on the bench beside her.

Romane leaned over. On Madison's screen, the number 13 had printed "not prime" fifty times in a column that ran right off the bottom of the window. Thirteen was prime; Madison had checked it on the divisibility chart taped to the cabin wall. Something invisible was going wrong inside her loop.

She read her code line by line, trying to isolate the problem. The loop went from 2 up to 12, checking whether any number divided 13 evenly. For each check that failed, she had typed a print statement saying "not prime." So the program printed it again and again, once for every number that did not divide 13.

"Twelve wrong answers instead of one right one," Zakary said from across the table, peering over. "You're punishing your program for being correct."

Madison laughed despite herself. She flipped her ponytail behind her shoulder and thought about the pattern. What she wanted was for the loop to quit the moment it found one divisor, and to stay quiet otherwise. Her eyes landed on a line in her notes from Tuesday's session with Ms. Islam: break.

"A break statement stops a loop immediately," she said slowly, reading her own handwriting. "So a prime checker can quit as soon as it finds a single divisor."

She restructured the code. Now the loop would only print "not prime" and then break if it found a divisor; if it finished every check without breaking, it would print "prime" exactly once. Her fingers felt elastic with nerves as she saved the file, and the clock over the door showed nineteen minutes remaining.

She typed 13 and pressed enter. The screen printed a single line: prime.

"Finally," Romane whispered, and patted the bench.

Ms. Islam walked the rows checking progress, pausing behind Madison's chair just long enough to read the output. "Twenty-eight," she said. "Try twenty-eight."

Madison entered it. The program printed "not prime" one time, then stopped, the loop abandoned mid-flight, its work finished early. She ran 97 next, and then 2, and each answer came back clean, single, correct.

When the showcase began on the porch, Madison stood up with her laptop. Zakary gave her a thumbs up, and Romane mouthed "go on." She set the computer on the rail where everyone could see and typed one more number.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The heart naturally speeds up a little on each breath in and slows down a little on each breath out, so slow breathing with long out-breaths helps the heart settle.
story:
The bathroom smelled like pink soap, and Rosalie had been standing at the sink for two full minutes with wet hands, waiting for her heart to stop hammering. In ten minutes she had to walk into the gym and run the assembly slide show in front of the whole sixth grade, because she had let Emelia delegate the tech job to her back when it seemed easy. It did not seem easy anymore. Her hands were cold, her stomach was a stone, and when she looked in the mirror her face was blotchy pink.

She wasn't even sure why she felt this bad. She knew the slides. She had practised twice. That was the part that scared her, actually, that something invisible was doing this to her body and she couldn't point at it.

The door creaked and Emelia slipped in, whispering, "Rosalie? Mr. Kim sent me to find you. He said if you're sick I have to take over." She hesitated in the doorway, taking in Rosalie's white knuckles on the sink. "Whoa. Okay. You're not sick, you're stressed."

"That's helpful," Rosalie said, but her voice came out thin.

Emelia came closer. "My little brother has this before every dentist visit. He does this thing he learned. Put two fingers on your wrist and feel your pulse." Rosalie did, feeling the quick thud, thud, thud. "Now breathe in slow." Rosalie breathed in, and under her fingers the pulse picked up, quicker. "Now out, longer than the in. Like counting to six." Rosalie let the breath go, slow and long, and the beat under her fingers stretched out, softened, slowed. Her heart speeds up a little on every breath in, she thought, and slows down on every breath out. Long out-breaths, then. That was the trick.

They did it together, Emelia counting quietly, "In... two... three... and out, four, five, six, seven." Three rounds of it, and the hammering in Rosalie's chest faded to something she could live with. The irony was not lost on her: she was hiding in a bathroom because of a slide show about healthy habits, of all things.

"One more thing," Emelia said as they pushed open the door. "My brother's thing includes last night. He never sleeps well before the dentist and it's always worse. So tonight you'll sleep, and tomorrow won't be like this."

The gym was loud and bright when they walked in together. Mr. Kim stood at the laptop, relief crossing his face. "There you are. Ready?"

Rosalie flexed her fingers, took one long breath out, and clicked the first slide forward.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee.
story:
The morning bus to the regional bee smelled like peanut butter and nerves. Alexa slid into the seat beside Ashwin, who was reading a folded note for the fourth time. "It's from Odin," he said. "He couldn't come, so he wrote you a pep talk. It's two pages. Front and back."

The note said: Dear Alexa, I know you're worried that only certain kinds of kids win spelling bees, like kids whose parents quiz them every night at dinner. You practice on the bus, which is way harder because the bus is bumpy and smells like peanut butter. Also, I looked up champions at the library yesterday for our bee project. In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee, and she also held three Guinness World Records for dribbling basketballs. So champions can be basketball people too, not just dinner-quiz people. Spell well. Your friend, Odin. P.S. I have changed my mind about the word "mnemonic." It is not pronounced "man-omic." Good luck.

Alexa read it twice, then stared out the window. She had been telling herself a story about spelling bee winners, a quiet little stereotype that lived in the back of her head: winners were kids with fancy word lists and private tutors, kids who practiced in silence, not kids like her. But if a girl who juggled basketballs could win the biggest bee in the country, then maybe the winning kind of kid was just many kinds of kid. Maybe the real pattern wasn't who you were. It was how you worked with words.

She decided to test it. At the library she had noticed that bee-winning words in recent years were often versatile ones, words that could show up in science or geography or old poems, so she had drilled those hardest. Now, on the bus, she asked Ashwin to quiz her only on words that could belong to more than one subject. "Fine," he said, "but if you get 'siphon' wrong I'm eating your spare pencil as a snack." She spelled siphon, and seismology, and brackish, and even mnemonic, which she pronounced correctly on purpose, just for Odin.

At the auditorium, Ms. Augustin checked them in and told Alexa to assess her confidence level honestly, because round one was worth staying calm for. Alexa said seven out of ten, which felt like a true number. Then she stood at the microphone, heard her word, and recognized it instantly as one of her versatile ones, the kind of word that could belong anywhere. She took a breath, looked at Ashwin holding up Odin's two-page note like a banner, and said, "S. I. P. H. O. N. Siphon."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
story:
Jasmine was sprawled on the living room rug with the tablet balanced on a cushion when the group chat lit up. Reagan had posted a poll: "Who thinks I should post the porch selfie? YES or YES." Below it sat the photo itself, sent twice, then a third time with the caption "vote now." In the picture Reagan stood on her front steps with her cat, Mr. Whiskers, draped over one shoulder like a scarf, and behind her the porch, the door, and a smudge of white near the railing.

Apollo replied first. "Mr. Whiskers gets my vote. Reagan also yes."

"It's a good picture," Jasmine typed, but she didn't send it yet. Something about the photo kept snagging her attention the way a loose thread catches on a zipper. She pinched the screen and the image magnified until the porch filled the whole display. There, sharp as anything, hung a little white sign next to the door with the number 14 on it, and on the mailbox post, the street name, Wren Street. Anyone in the chat, and anyone the photo got sent to after that, could see exactly where Reagan lived.

She scrolled back through the chat's history to test her idea. Last month Reagan had posted a picture from the school gym, and behind her, stretched across the wall, was the banner with the school's name and mascot. A week before that, a shot at the park with the sign for Wren Street Lake in the corner. Every picture carried its own address, like a return label nobody noticed sticking on.

"Reagan," Jasmine typed, "zoom in on the door in your selfie."

"why"

"Just do it. Look at the sign."

The typing bubble appeared, vanished, appeared again. Then: "oh. that's my house number."

"A stranger could work out where the photo was taken," Jasmine wrote. "Street sign, house number, even the school logo. You've basically posted your address three times."

"I want likes," Reagan replied. "Poppy from summer camp said she'd share it with her whole cabin. That's like twelve people."

Apollo sent a single line of laughing emojis. "Poppy's cabin follows everybody. They followed a pigeon account once."

Jasmine sat up, thinking. The chat was seven kids, but posts could be forwarded, saved, shared on, and once a photo left this little group it was like water going through a net. You couldn't pull it back. "Crop the picture," she suggested. "Cut off everything past the door. Keep you and Mr. Whiskers."

There was a long pause, long enough for Jasmine to notice the porch light was on outside her own window and that her father was humming in the kitchen, steering his way through a new recipe the way a boat drifts without a rudder whenever he stopped reading the instructions.

The edited photo arrived. Reagan stood in a tight square of just steps and cat, background trimmed away, number gone, street name gone. "New poll," she wrote. "Who thinks Mr. Whiskers should have his own account? YES or YES."

"ME," said Apollo.

Jasmine hit send on "Mr. Whiskers 2024" and went to find her father, because from the smell of it, the soup had gone past porous crackers to something resembling paste.

activity: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
knowledge_domain: to use pivot tables in a spreadsheet to summarise survey answers by grade
fact: In Excel, the PivotTable Fields pane has four areas, Filters, Columns, Rows and Values, and dragging a field into an area decides where it appears in the table.
story:
Cameron had surveyed the whole school about lunch food, 214 answers, and now all that data sat on his laptop like a lake that had swallowed a picnic. He wanted to know one thing: which grade liked pizza the most. Heinrich had bet him a candy bar that seventh graders would win, and Cameron intended to collect.

His first attempt was a disaster. He clicked something called PivotTable, and a new empty grid appeared beside a strange floating pane. He dragged the word "Grade" into the middle of the sheet and nothing happened, which felt deeply unfair. Then he dragged "Food" somewhere random and the grid filled with numbers that made no sense at all. Row after row of soggy mystery. "You look like you're trying to drown your own spreadsheet," said his dad from the kitchen doorway.

"The data is submerging me," Cameron said. "Two hundred answers. Zero patterns."

He looked harder at the floating pane. It had four boxes stacked on top of each other, labeled Filters, Columns, Rows and Values, and each box was a slot you could drop a field into. So the pane wasn't just decoration; it was the machine's control panel, and where you dropped a field decided where it showed up in the table. That was a logical way to build a thing, actually. On purpose, he dragged "Grade" into Rows, and the grades listed themselves down the side, six through eight. He tried to drag "Food" into Columns and missed, dropping it into Filters by mistake, and the whole table went blank. He fished it back out. "Filters," he muttered. "So that's what you're for. Not yet."

"Food" landed in Columns at last, and food names marched across the top. Then he dragged "Grade" a second copy, wait, no, he dragged "Answer" into Values, and numbers bloomed everywhere, one count for every grade and every food. There it was, the pattern he couldn't see in the raw lake of answers: pizza row, grade by grade. Seventh grade: forty-one votes. Sixth grade: thirty-six. Eighth grade: thirty-eight.

Cameron took a photo of the screen and texted Heinrich. "Start buying the candy bar." Heinrich replied with a single groaning emoji and the message, "check eighth grade tacos tho." Cameron checked. Eighth grade tacos: forty-four, the highest number in the whole table. Nobody had bet on tacos. "New bet," Cameron typed. "Whoever's grade loses has to eat cafeteria tacos all week." Heinrich answered fast: "Deal. And don't submerge me in screenshots, I already saw it." Cameron dragged "Food" into Filters anyway and clicked taco, just to watch the table rearrange itself one more time.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
Xavier stood at the counter with the recipe spread in front of him, a lemony chicken and a big green salad to go with it. His parents would be home at seven, and he wanted dinner ready, not started. He had already sliced the raw chicken breast into strips and scraped them into the sizzling pan. Now he pulled a head of romaine from the fridge and reached for the cutting board, the same one, because it was right there.

He paused, knife in hand. Something about the board bothered him. It looked clean enough, just a few wet smears, but he kept thinking about the chicken juice that had pooled on it a minute ago. Ms. Nielsen had mentioned something once, in the middle of a unit on food safety that most of the class had half slept through. He remembered copying a phrase into his notes, and he dug the crumpled page out of his backpack right there on the kitchen floor.

"Cross-contamination," he read aloud. Raw meat on one board, ready-to-eat food on another, so bacteria from the meat couldn't spread to food that would never touch a flame. That was the whole idea. The lettuce would go straight from board to bowl to table, no cooking, no heat, nothing to stop whatever the chicken had left behind. He turned the wooden board over and squinted at the knife marks. Could stuff hide in those grooves, even after a rinse? It seemed possible, and he didn't want to test it on his family.

So he washed the board in hot, soapy water and set it in the rack, then took the clean plastic one from the cabinet for the salad. He chopped the romaine, diced a tomato, and whisked oil and vinegar in a jar. He decided to incorporate some leftover corn and a handful of croutons, which made the salad look like a real restaurant's. He wondered whether the raw-chicken rule was why restaurants had boards in different colors, and made a mental note to ask Georges, whose family ran a diner.

At seven, his parents walked in sniffing the air. His dad peeked at the pan, and his mom lifted the salad bowl and turned it appreciatively.

"Two cutting boards?" she asked, nodding at the dish rack.

"Yep," Xavier said. "Chicken gets one, salad gets the other. Cross-contamination."

"Where'd you learn that?"

He shrugged and grinned. "School. Who wants salad?"

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: A 2006 study by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it.
story:
The spelling bee was three weeks away, and Michael had a plan: read the list of four hundred words every single night until his eyes knew every letter.
