He read it on the bus, he read it at lunch, and he read it under his blanket with a flashlight until his mother made him sleep. By Friday, his paper had gone brittle at the folds from being opened and closed so many times.

"Quiz me," said Jethro, sliding into the seat next to him before class.

"I don't need quizzing," Michael said. "I've read the list six times."

Jethro shrugged. "Okay. Spell reconnaissance."

Michael opened his mouth. Nothing came out. He could picture the page, the smudge in the corner, even the coffee ring near the top, but the letters had gone blurry in his mind. He tried to retrieve the word and got only "R, E, C" before he stopped, cheeks hot.

"That's what I thought," Jethro said. "My sister made me look something up last year. There was a study in 2006, by Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke, and they found that testing yourself on material helps you remember it longer than simply rereading it."

"Rereading feels like studying, though," Michael said.

"That's the trap," Jethro said.

That night, Michael handed the list to his mother and made her quiz him out loud. It was worse than reading. He missed chrysanthemum, he missed ghastliness, he missed parallel twice. But every time he got one wrong, she made him spell it three times before moving on, and the misses stung in a way that made them stick.

Ms. Gill held the class bee on a Thursday, and the gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn from the cafeteria. Jane went out on silhouette and gave Michael a thumbs up on her way to her seat. Round by round, the words came, and Michael found that the ones he had missed at his kitchen table now arrived in his head whole, letter by letter, like lights switching on down a hallway.

At the microphone, facing "irresistible," Michael thought of his mother tapping the counter with her pen, night after night, and he smiled. He didn't hear the word from a page in his mind. He heard her voice asking for it.

"I R R E S I S T I B L E," he said.

"Correct," said Ms. Gill. "One word left for the win."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
story:
The living room was so full that Hailey had to share the corner of the couch with Elliot, while Landen sat on the floor with a plate balanced on his knees. Everyone was shouting at the screen when the receiver landed in the end zone and the referee waved his arms, signaling incomplete. "His foot was in!" Hailey's grandfather bellowed, spraying popcorn. "They'll show it again," her dad said, and sure enough, the network ran the play back, once in slow motion, once from a second angle. The foot was clearly in bounds, and the whole room roared when the call got reversed.

"Rewind it again," Elliot begged, as if the remote were magic. Grandpa laughed and said something that snagged in Hailey's mind. "You kids think TV always could do that. When I was young, if you missed a play, it was gone. Vanished." Landen frowned. "That can't be right. They replay everything now." Grandpa shrugged. "Somebody had to invent it. I just don't remember who."

Hailey couldn't stop wondering. Somebody had to be first, on some specific day, at some specific game, and it seemed strange that something so ordinary had a beginning nobody in the room knew. She tested a simple idea: if it was a big deal, it would be written down somewhere, the way first flights and first telephone calls were. She borrowed her dad's phone, told him what she was hunting for, and typed in the words instant replay first used. Elliot leaned over her shoulder, and Landen climbed up onto the couch arm so he could see too.

"There," Hailey said, holding the screen out so even Grandpa could read it. The first instant replay in a live sports broadcast happened on December 7, 1963, during the Army-Navy football game, and the director who made it happen was CBS's Tony Verna. "December seventh," Grandpa repeated slowly. "Army-Navy. I would have been about that age." He shook his head, half grinning. "Fifty years I've been watching, and I never once wondered when it started."

Landen turned to Hailey's dad. "Would they even permit something like that today, a director just trying a brand new thing in the middle of a live game?" "Probably not," Dad said. "Too risky. One mistake in front of millions." "So Tony Verna had a reputation for taking chances," Elliot said, and Grandpa snorted, "No, kid, he made one that day." Hailey grinned and passed the popcorn down to Landen, who had the least of anybody, and Grandpa handed Elliot the last soda without being asked.

On the screen the stadium roared through another replay, and Grandpa pointed at the television with his remote. "That machine is keeping history alive," he said. "Rewind it one more time."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: When smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.
story:
Alexandre stood in front of the mirror in the boys' bathroom, holding a stopwatch, and said, "Hello, brain, I have arrived." Nehemiah leaned against the sink and clicked the timer. "Two seconds. Your mouth is closer to your brain than a cigarette is. Barely."

They had a problem. Ms. Ivanova had assigned each pair in health class one question to answer for the fifth graders, and Alexandre and Nehemiah had drawn the worst one: why do people get addicted to nicotine? Briar had gotten "why do your ears pop," which she said was basically a vacation. Alexandre wanted his presentation to be the one the little kids actually remembered, and he had exactly one fact written on his notecard: when smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.

"That can't be right," Nehemiah said on the way back to class. "I sat next to my grandpa on a six-hour flight. Nothing happened in 10 seconds for that man except sweating."

"Everything about him is slow," Alexandre said. "The doctor told my mom his cartilage is basically vintage. That's not the same as his blood."

They turned into Ms. Ivanova's room, where she was stacking diagrams of a brain on the front table. "Ten seconds," Alexandre said. "Nicotine gets to the brain in about 10 seconds after someone inhales. That's faster than I can find a pencil."

"Look it up in the actual textbook instead of telling me at speed," Ms. Ivanova said, but she said it while sliding the book across the table toward him, which Alexandre took as a good sign.

He and Nehemiah tested the idea at lunch. Alexandre put a random jellybean in his mouth and Nehemiah timed how long until Alexandre could taste it, which was not the same thing at all, Alexandre admitted, but it proved the general principle that stuff travels fast when there's a direct route. Then they tried it again, because the first jellybean was green and Alexandre wanted a do-over. "This is not science," Nehemiah said, eating a third one himself. "This is lunch with a stopwatch."

For the presentation, Alexandre had a plan. He would have five fifth graders stand in a line from the front door of the classroom to the back wall, and he would walk the route while Nehemiah counted the seconds out loud. He practiced the walk twice during recess and got it down to 9 seconds, which he decided was close enough and also extremely satisfying.

On presentation day, Briar went first with her ears-popping talk, which did turn out to be a vacation, and then Alexandre pointed at the door. "Breathe in," he told the fifth graders. "Right now, inhale." They all did, one kid so hard he coughed. Nehemiah started counting, and Alexandre walked the line of kids while the numbers climbed, one, two, three, tapping each of them on the shoulder like a relay. At eight he reached the wall, where Briar had taped a paper brain. At ten, he slapped it.

"That's how fast it happens," Alexandre said. "Ten seconds, and the nicotine's already there, in the brain, in the part that handles rewards. So the brain learns: that thing I did, do it again."

A fifth grader in the front row raised her hand. "My uncle does it the second he's stressed."

"Ten seconds," Alexandre said. "Every time." He tapped the paper brain once more, just for luck.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: According to the CDC, nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18.
story:
Jade had signed up for the camp's science showcase thinking she would get to build a volcano. Instead the topic card she drew from Mr. Virtanen's hat read, "How nicotine hooks the brain." Worse, she had forty-eight hours to figure it out, and her only teammates were Gia, who wanted to do a rap about it, and Sawyer, who was currently eating the marshmallows meant for the volcano group.

"You can't rap about neurons," Jade said, flipping through the camp library's one health textbook under a buzzing porch light. "Nobody even knows what a neuron is."

"That's why it's educational," Gia said.

Sawyer leaned over her shoulder, smelling like burnt sugar. "Here's what I don't get. If nicotine is bad for you, why would anyone keep doing it? Your brain isn't stupid."

That was the question, Jade realized, and the answer wasn't in the room. It was hidden inside a skull, too small to see, and she couldn't exactly peek. She persevered through three chapters, chewing her pencil until it tasted like splinters, while mosquitos whined against the screen door. Somewhere in the middle of chapter nine, something clicked. Nicotine, she read, tricked the brain's reward pathway, the system that said "do that again" when you ate a good meal or won a race. Nicotine hijacked it. That was why quitting was so hard: the brain itself had been taught to want more.

The next morning a folded note slid under the cabin door, smelling faintly of the lake. Jade opened it. "Ask the nurse about the nine out of ten thing. Trust me. Signed, a mysterious stranger." Below, in handwriting she absolutely recognized as Gia's, it added, "P.S. It's me, Gia. The nurse is only at the infirmary until lunch."

The nurse, a cheerful woman with a bandana, dug out a laminated sheet from a battered folder. "CDC numbers," she said. "Nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18." She tapped the page. "Think about that one yourself. I'm not allowed to hand you your whole project."

Jade stood in the doorway, the fact turning over in her head like a key in a lock. Nine out of ten. Grown-ups, hooked, and it started before eighteen. Before her age. It was a significant clue: if the brain's reward pathway was still developing in teenagers, then what started young could grab on hard and last for decades. Companies that sold cigarettes had every reason to care about people her age. That was the insight Sawyer's question had been pointing at all along.

At the showcase, under the picnic pavilion, Jade laid out her poster: a drawing of a brain with a little cartoon nicotine molecule pressing the "again, again" button. "Imagine a hijacker in the driver's seat," she said, "except the car is your brain." Gia performed one verse of the rap anyway, which rhymed "reward pathway" with "your brain gets a delay, hey," and even Mr. Virtanen laughed.

Sawyer raised his hand. "So why do companies aim ads at us?"

Jade held up the laminated sheet. "Nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18," she said. "They're not advertising to the smokers they have. They're advertising to the smokers they want."

Mr. Virtanen stopped laughing and wrote something in his notebook, and Gia whispered, "Told you the rap helped."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Repeating a measurement several times and taking the average gives a more reliable result than a single try.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and cut grass, and Leah had cleared a lane down the middle of it with two broom handles laid flat as rails. Her science-fair project was due Thursday, and the plan was simple: roll a tennis ball from the workbench, time it with a stopwatch, measure how far it went, and draw a distance-time graph. Ariel sat on an upturned milk crate holding the stopwatch, chewing her pen, because she wanted the job of timer. She had said so twice on the walk over.

"Three, two, one, go," Ariel called. Leah released the ball. It wobbled along the broom handles, past the recycling bins, and knocked softly against the garage door. Ariel clicked the stopwatch and wrote the number on the clipboard: 2.1 seconds for four meters. They did it again. 2.0 seconds. Again. 2.2. Leah plotted each dot on her graph paper, and a line was starting to show, tidy and climbing.

Then the fourth roll went wrong. The ball seemed to hesitate near the paint cans, and the stopwatch read 3.4 seconds. Leah's stomach dropped. She plotted the dot anyway, and it sat far below the others like a stone in a pond. Her whole graph would bend toward it. Tomorrow she had to stand in the gymnasium and explain a crooked line to Mr. Côté.

"That's it," Ariel said, clicking the pen shut. "One weird roll. Just erase it."

Leah stared at the dot. She thought about her neighbor, who had once judged a whole jar of pennies by weighing one handful, and how wrong he had been until he weighed three. She didn't want to erase. "Let's roll five more times," she said. "Same distance, same everything."

Ariel groaned but reset the stopwatch. They rolled and rolled. The readings came in at 2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 2.1, 2.0. None of them looked anything like 3.4. Leah wrote all six numbers in a column and found the average, adding them up and dividing by six. The average was close to 2.1 seconds, and the odd reading barely moved it. It was a small insight with a radical effect on her graph: the line straightened, and the strange dot sat alone below it, obviously wrong, obviously not the ball's real speed.

"Why was that one so slow, though?" Ariel asked.

Leah crouched beside the paint cans. The concrete there was rough, and something small and dark was wedged in a crack. She pried it out with her fingernail. A pebble, sharp-edged, exactly where the ball had slowed. The hidden cause had been sitting there the whole time, invisible until she looked for it.

She dropped the pebble into her pocket, because she wanted it taped to her poster board as evidence. "Average of six rolls," she said, and wrote it in big letters at the bottom of the graph. Then she flicked the ball down the lane one more time, just to watch it run clean.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
story:
The lights at the farmhouse went out at suppertime, right in the middle of Connor's math homework. He heard his dad groan from the kitchen and the dog start barking at nothing. Connor found the flashlight in the hall drawer, then dug out a second one and carried it to his little sister, who was sitting very still on the stairs, afraid of the dark.

His dad was already out in the garage, dragging the portable generator toward the middle of the floor. Connor stood in the doorway and watched him set it down near the workbench, close to the door that opened into the kitchen. Dad was reaching for the pull cord when Connor's stomach did a small pivot, the kind it did before a race. Something was wrong here, and he was hesitant to say so, because Dad hated being corrected. Still, his mouth rebelled against staying shut.

"Dad, wait."

"What? Freezing's going to set in, buddy."

"Mr. Ngo did a whole unit on this in science. Generators give off carbon monoxide, so you have to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows. Never in a house or a garage. That's exactly what he said." Connor pointed at the garage walls around them. "And this is a garage."

Dad's hand stayed on the cord. He looked at the generator, then at the kitchen door, then at his son. "Your teacher say that?"

"Twice. He made us repeat it. He said the same rule goes for charcoal grills, too. Outdoors only, away from everything."

Dad straightened up and let out a long breath. "Well. Suppose I'd rather look slightly foolish than extremely sorry." He tipped the generator onto its wheels and rolled it out through the big garage door, across the gravel, and down near the fence at the far edge of the yard. Connor followed with the extension cord coiled over his shoulder, unspooling it behind them. They ran the cord through the window well, and when Dad pulled the cord, the generator coughed to life under the open sky, a safe distance from every door and window of the house.

Inside, a lamp clicked on and his sister whooped from the stairs. Dad set about lighting the gas stove, since the oven wouldn't work, and heated up a pot of soup while Connor spread a blanket on the living room floor. His sister settled between them with her flashlight balanced on her knee like a camp lantern.

Dad slurped his soup, then nudged Connor's elbow. "Tell Mr. Ngo he probably just kept this family warm and safe tonight, all at the same time."

"I'll tell him Monday," Connor said, and passed his sister the last of the bread.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
Olivier posted the photo at 4:32 on a Saturday afternoon, standing between the escalators at the mall with his shoe halfway into the fountain. Darren had dared him, and Sonia had been laughing so hard she dropped her slushie. He captioned it "mall fountain legend" and tagged the location, then went to look at sneakers.

At 4:42 he thought better of it. Ms. Chatterjee, his neighbour, shopped at this mall every Saturday, and she knew his mother. He deleted the post, watched it vanish from his page, and felt fine about it. The photo had been up for ten minutes, which seemed like nothing.

On Sunday morning it was in the grade eight group chat. Sonia sent it to him first with a row of question marks. "I deleted that," he typed. "I know," she replied. "Darren screenshotted it before you did. So did three other people, I think." He scrolled up. There it was, with his face and the fountain and the location tag, saved on phones that were not his.

He called Darren. "Why did you keep it?"

"You deleted it, but I already had it," Darren said. "Deleting a post takes it off your page. It doesn't take it off my phone."

Olivier sat with that. So the delete button only cleaned his side of the street. Anything anyone had grabbed was still out there, in their cameras and their chats, and he could not reach any of it. He tried an experiment. He posted a second photo, a boring one of the food court, and asked Darren to screenshot it. Then he deleted it and asked Darren to send the screenshot back. It arrived in four seconds, whole and sharp. The page said the post no longer existed; the copy said otherwise.

On Monday he did a small survey at his locker, trying to be impartial about it instead of just embarrassed. He asked eleven kids whether they thought deleting a post made it gone. Nine said yes. Those nine, he realized, were the same nine who never covered their locker combinations with a hand. He sorted the results into a category he labelled "checks phone, believes phone" and showed Sonia the tally.

"Ms. Chatterjee is in the group chat," Sonia said suddenly, staring at her screen. "Her niece added her. She can see everything."

Olivier looked at the photo of his shoe in the fountain, now viewed by a woman who waved to him over the fence every morning. He pulled out his phone and typed, "Hi Ms. Chatterjee."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
The war memorial sat on a hill above the school, its stone arch symmetrical on both sides, with names carved in neat rows. Autumn had a clipboard, a borrowed book from the library, and forty minutes before Ms. Sadeghi's class presentation on why settlers moved west in the 1800s. She had planned to be ready last night, but her poster had collapsed when the glue failed, and now she was rebuilding her whole argument.

Eliott was already there, sitting on the memorial's bottom step with his laptop open. "You brought the textbook?" he asked. Autumn dropped her bag beside him. "Ms. Sadeghi said we have to use a primary source," she said. "I think this counts." She pulled out the library book, a reprint of a diary written by a settler woman crossing the trail, and next to it her modern textbook chapter with its tidy maps.

Mouhamed came running up the hill, out of breath. "The bell rings in half an hour," he panted. "Is it true she won't accept the assignment late?"

Autumn looked down at the diary. The woman had written about bad harvests back home and how her husband wanted new land for agriculture, and how her sister had gone ahead the year before and sent letters that never said to come but never said not to, either. The textbook said the same thing in one flat paragraph: people moved west for farmland and opportunity. It was quicker. It was cleaner. She had quoted it twice in her first draft, and she wondered now whether she had done that because it was easier, or because she had not really understood what she was supposed to find.

"Okay, I have to decide," she said. She laid both books on the flat top of the memorial's base, where the carved names made a line between them. "The diary was written by the person who lived it, at the time. The textbook was written way later by somebody studying it. So the diary is the primary source, and the textbook is the secondary source." Eliott looked up from his laptop. "That's the word she used. Primary source. So quote the diary."

"Show me," Mouhamed said, leaning over her shoulder. Autumn read aloud the entry from October, where the woman wrote that the river had flooded their fields again and they would violate their lease if they stayed and could not pay, so they were leaving in the spring. Three sentences, and they said more than the whole textbook page. The diarist had not explained her reasons in a summary. She had mentioned a flood in passing, a worry about money, a sister out west, all mixed together with a headache and a broken wagon wheel.

"I almost used the easy one," Autumn admitted. She copied the entry onto a fresh card, word for word, and underlined the flood. "Last night I picked the textbook because it was faster. That was a mistake, I think. Or maybe not a mistake, just the lazy road." Mouhamed shrugged. "You found the diary eventually." Autumn packed the books, and the three of them started down the hill toward the school. Halfway down, she stopped and flipped her card over to add one more line, then ran to catch up. "First one to the door gets my extra granola bar," she called.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The sports bar smelled like fried pickles and shouted opinions, and Alexa slid into the booth between her dad and her little brother, who was already poking at the wall of televisions. On the biggest screen a commentator was saying that a quarterback had thrown for a "near-perfect 156.7." Her dad nodded like he knew exactly what that meant, but her brother frowned.

"Perfect should be a hundred," he said. "Like on a test."

Dad waved a wing at the screen. "Ratings are out of a hundred, buddy. That guy just rounds up."

Alexa didn't think that was right. She had watched the same commentator last week say "a perfect 158.3," and she remembered the number because it looked like somebody's street address, not like a score. A perfect score that wasn't 100 felt like a rule hiding somewhere, and hidden rules bothered her the way a pebble in a shoe bothered her foot. She pulled out her phone and typed "perfect quarterback rating."

Rayne, who had come with her own parents for the Sunday games, leaned over from the next booth. "Whatcha looking up?"

"Trying to conquer a weird number," Alexa said. On the screen, a stat box flashed: completions, attempts, yards, touchdowns, interceptions, all squashed at the end into one big bold number. That was the strange part, she realized. The commentator never mentioned the four little stats again, just the final figure, like they had all been squeezed through a funnel.

The page loaded. She read it twice, then turned the phone toward her dad. "It's called passer rating," she said. "It takes a bunch of passing statistics and combines them into one number, and the scale goes from zero all the way up to a maximum of 158.3."

Her dad squinted at the screen, then at his wing, then back. "Huh. I've been calling it a percentage for years."

"It's not a percentage at all," Alexa said. "It just gets talked about like one. And they rank the quarterbacks by it, so one guy ends up above another guy because of a number that has like four things packed inside it."

"So a hundred isn't perfect," her brother said slowly, like he was deciding whether to be annoyed or impressed. "One fifty-eight point three is."

"That's actually kind of cool," Dad admitted, and he raised his soda toward the screen. "To the weird number."

"Also," Rayne said, grinning, "your team's quarterback is ranked ninth, so maybe don't celebrate too hard."

Dad groaned and covered his eyes. Alexa slid her a handful of napkins and started copying the little stats from the screen. "We'll do the guy from your team next," she said. "Number two in the whole league."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Islam teaches that on the Day of Judgment, called Yawm al-Qiyamah, all people will be raised and judged, and sent to paradise or hell.
story:
Elijah arrived at his aunt's backyard barbecue carrying a shoebox of index cards, because Mr. Baptiste's assignment was due Tuesday and he had promised himself he would finish it before the potato salad ran out. The project asked students to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and he had picked Islam and Hinduism. His problem was simpler and more urgent: he had twenty-two cards, two religions, and no idea how to make the comparison fair.

His cousin Miller spotted the box before Elijah even set it down. "Is that the project? Can I help? I want to be in education when I grow up, so I need teaching experience." Miller was nine and announced his future career roughly once a week, but he was persistent, and Elijah was short on helpers.

They spread the cards on the picnic table between the bean dip and the watermelon. Some cards came from interviews Elijah had done. One, written in his uncle's careful handwriting, said that in Islam each person lives one life, and after death waits for the Day of Judgment. "It's called Yawm al-Qiyamah," his uncle said, drifting over with a plate of ribs. "That's the day everyone is raised and judged, and then sent to paradise or hell." He took a rib and wandered off, leaving Elijah to stare at the card.

"Okay," Miller said. "So how do we organize these?"

Elijah tried sorting the cards by topic first, then by religion, then by which ones had the word "judgment" on them. It kept going wrong. Finally he had an idea he could actually test. "What if we classify them by the number of lives? Islam says one. Hinduism says many. That's the whole difference, right there." He made two piles and held them side by side. One pile had a single straight line: live, die, wait, be raised, be judged, go to paradise or hell. The other pile looped back on itself, life after life after life.

From across the yard, their neighbor Mr. Baptiste, who had come for the pie, leaned over the table. "Careful with that looping pile," he said, tapping it. "Some of my students think reincarnation looks sinister on paper, like a trap. Then they talk to my aunt, who explains it as a journey. Same drawing, different feeling." He smiled at the watermelon. "That's your real comparison, by the way. Not just what happens, but how each story treats getting there."

Elijah wrote "one life, one judgment" beside the first pile and "many lives" beside the second, then drew the straight line and the loop. Miller copied the chart onto a napkin and announced he had "basically co-taught this."

"You made a treaty with me," Miller said. "Helpers get first dessert."

"That was never the treaty," Elijah said, but he was already handing him a slice of pie.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: In the most basic twelve-bar blues, the band stays on the I chord for the first four bars and moves to the IV chord in bar five.
story:
Jack had the twelve-bar blues written on a folded sheet of paper, and he had memorized it wrong, though he did not know that yet. Ms. Foster had put the school's rhythm section together in the music room after last bell: a drummer named Shea, a bass player named Madilyn, and Jack on trumpet, which he had only picked up in September.

"Count the bars," Ms. Foster said. "Don't watch your fingers. Listen to the bass." Then she sat at the piano to comp chords and left the rest to them.

Jack's solo started well. He found a few notes that swaggered, low and bent, and Shea's drums pushed him forward like a hand between his shoulder blades. The music room windows were open, and the sound went out over the estuary behind the school, where the river met the tide in wide brown channels. Jack closed his eyes and thought about that meeting of waters, and he lifted his solo up, reaching for the change.

The change did not come. Madilyn kept plowing along on the same deep note, and Jack's high, bright line landed on top of it like a shoe on a birthday cake. The sound was ugly and distinct, one layer clashing against another, and his ears burned even before he opened his eyes.

"Bar five," Madilyn said, not unkindly. "You went up in four."

"But the pattern repeats every four bars," Jack said. "I counted it."

"That's what contradicts you, though," she said. "In the most basic twelve-bar blues, the band stays on the I chord for the first four bars and moves to the IV chord in bar five." She tapped her bass. "Four bars home, then one bar of change. You have to wait me out."

Jack unfolded his paper and looked at the chart again, and there it was, plain as a stop sign, the IV printed at the top of the fifth bar. He had counted in fours and assumed the harmony counted in fours too. It did not. The band held home longer than he expected, and that was the whole secret.

"Let me try again," he said. "Shea, count the bars out loud."

They ran it twice more. The first time, Jack watched Madilyn's left hand and let her fingers tell him where the harmony lived, and though his solo was careful, almost timid, nothing crashed. The second time he closed his eyes again, and this time he waited. One, two, three, four bars of the low home chord, and only then, on five, when Madilyn's hand shifted, he rose with it, and his line and hers braided together over the drums.

At the end Ms. Foster wrote something on a sticky note and put it on his music stand before she left the room. "That last chorus," it said, "is the one. Same time Thursday."

Jack folded the note into his pocket next to the chart, put his trumpet in its case, and clicked the latches shut.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
Norah spread the photocopied diary pages across the library table and flattened the curling corner with her pencil box. The assignment from Ms. Goh said one thing in bold letters: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The diary, written by a settler named Hannah Barlow in 1846, was supposed to be her evidence. The trouble was that Hannah Barlow wrote about everything, from spoiled bacon to her sister's wedding, and Norah had until Friday to make sense of it.

"Find anything?" Cassia dropped into the chair opposite, holding a page so close to her face that her breath fogged the plastic sleeve. "I just found the word precipitation in here. She complains about it twice. That's my exciting discovery of the day."

"Great. Weather complaints." Norah slid a page across. "I need actual reasons, not complaints."

Jazmin arrived with three granola bars and sat down. "Ms. Goh said my last draft was, quote, competent but not convincing." She tore open a wrapper. "Which is teacher for boring. So I'm starting over, and I'm taking your diary leftovers."

At home that night, Norah read the diary again with a pencil, underlining every line where Hannah explained a decision. On the fourth page, Hannah wrote that the family's Missouri neighbors had all left after the banks failed and the bugs took the corn two years running. On the fifth page, Hannah's father said Oregon soil was supposed to be so rich a man could grow anything, and that land there was nearly free for the asking. Norah stopped. The failures were pushing the family out of Missouri. The land was pulling them toward Oregon. She wrote two columns on a scrap of paper and started sorting every reason she'd underlined into one or the other.

The next morning she showed the columns to Cassia and Jazmin before class. "Push reasons and pull reasons," she said. "The bugs push them out of Missouri, and the free land pulls them west."

"Those are called push factors and pull factors," Cassia said, without looking up from her page. "It was on the board yesterday when you were sharpening your pencil for ten minutes."

"You watched me sharpen a pencil and said nothing?"

"It was a very good pencil. Also, I have this line where Hannah writes she'd rather be eaten by bears in Oregon than stay one more winter in Missouri. Which column is the bear?"

"That's not a factor, that's a mood," Jazmin said, and laughed so hard Ms. Goh looked over from her desk.

On Friday, Norah stood at the front of the room with the diary pages clipped to a poster of her two columns. "I cite the entry from April 1846, where Hannah Barlow writes that the banks failed and the corn was ruined," she said, pointing to the left column, "and the entry from May, where her father describes free land in Oregon." She tapped the right column. "The family was pushed out of Missouri and pulled west, and both kinds of reasons show up in her own words." She stepped back and looked at the poster, then at the class, and waited for the first question.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
Jacob spread three cereal boxes across the library table and frowned at them. His problem was real: the school was holding a contest for the best advertisement for the library's new reading club, and the winning poster would hang in the front hall for a whole year. He wanted that spot badly. Mr. Yoon, the librarian, had told the class to persuade people, and Jacob had discovered, after an hour of staring at boxes shouting "NEW!" and "EVERYONE LOVES IT!", that he had no idea how persuasion actually worked.

Selena dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books. "You look like the boxes insulted you."

"They kind of did. Look at this one. 'Everybody's switching to Crunch-O's.' If everybody switched, why does it need a giant ad?" Jacob turned the box toward her. "And this says 'criminally delicious.' What does that even mean?" He copied the phrases onto his notepad, one per line, and then wrote a heading above them: tricks?

Selena leaned in. "My brother calls that a bandwagon appeal. The ad wants you to feel left out."

That word, bandwagon, snagged something in Jacob's memory. He flashed back to last fall, when his class had stood in the World War II gallery at the museum, in front of a wall of old government posters. He remembered the crowd of faces, the bold colors, the slogans repeating the same idea over and over. Selena had read the placard beside them out loud, slowly, because the words were long. "In March 1933," she had said, "Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda." A whole ministry, just for persuasion, Jacob had thought at the time. Then Matias had whispered, "Public enlightenment and propaganda? Those are basically opposites stuck together," and they had all stood there a little longer than they needed to.

Back at the library table, Jacob had an idea he could actually test. He wrote two identical posters on scrap paper: JOIN THE READING CLUB, and EVERYONE'S ALREADY IN THE READING CLUB, DON'T MISS OUT, plus one celebrity line, "Matias says it's awesome." He showed both to a sixth grader walking past the returns desk and asked which made her want to join. She pointed at the second one instantly. Then he swapped the loaded words out for plain ones and asked again. She hesitated and picked the plain poster. So the tricks worked, he thought, but only when they were there, like lights on a machine. A whole network of posters and radio spots had done the same thing in 1933, and it hadn't been for cereal.

He pulled out a clean sheet. He would advocate for the reading club, but with a poster that showed real kids and real books, not a fake crowd. When he started sketching, the faces he drew were the ones he actually saw every Tuesday: Selena with her stack, Matias with the graphic novels, the sixth grader by the desk.

Mr. Yoon paused behind them on his way past. "Now that one," he said, tapping the blank corner of the page, "I'd put in the front hall."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up.
story:
Aria pushed the flashlight closer to the basketball she had propped on a stack of dictionaries. Her presentation for science was due Friday, and she had decided to explain why Earth's tilt causes the seasons by acting them out in her living room. She tilted the basketball with a chopstick taped to its side, marked a dot for their city, and walked the whole setup around the lamp on the coffee table. When the dot leaned toward the light, the beam landed bright and concentrated. When it leaned away, the same beam spread thin and pale. So far, so good.

The problem showed up on slide four. She had written "June 21, the longest day of the year, is the hottest day of the year," and something about it nagged at her. She remembered August. She remembered lying on the kitchen floor last August with every fan in the house pointed at her, while in late June she had still been wearing a sweatshirt in the mornings. She frowned at the slide. Maybe her memory was just vague, mixed up from too many summers mashed together.

She called Jeremiah, who kept a thermometer log on his windowsill for a project he never finished. "Read me your numbers," she said, and he did, digging through a crumpled notebook while his little sister shouted about markers in the background. The highest temperatures were all from the end of July and the first weeks of August. "So the longest day isn't the hottest," Aria said slowly. "The hottest weeks come later, after the longest day." Jeremiah said that sounded wrong, and then said he had to go find the markers before his sister drew on the wall.

Aria sat with the flashlight and the basketball a long time. She tried to evaluate her whole presentation, not just slide by slide but as a story that would make sense to Sabrina, who asked a question about everything. Land and oceans must take time to warm up, she realized, the way the lake near her grandmother's house stayed cold into July even when the air was warm. The heat built up slowly and hung around. She deleted the wrong sentence and typed a new one, then changed her last slide so it ended with a question for the class instead of a fact she hadn't checked.

There was a knock, and Mr. Liu from next door stood on the porch holding a plate of plum slices because his tree had gone wild again. Aria took the plate and, without really planning to, told him about the basketball and the flashlight and the temperature chart. He laughed and said his tomatoes never came in until well after the longest day of the year either, no matter what he did.

"Here," Aria said, picking up the flashlight again. "Want to see Earth go around the sun? It only takes a minute."
